summary: Gives guidance for locating the resources associated with the im and pres URI schemes defined by the Common Profiles for Presence and Instant Messaging. It explains how to resolve these addresses to find the right service.

plainLanguage.summary: Like using a phone book to find where a friend lives, this document tells chat systems how to find the right place for an address.

questions: how to find an instant messaging server from an im uri
how to resolve an im uri
what is the pres uri scheme
how does srv lookup work for instant messaging
subtitle: How a client turns an im: or pres: address into the server to contact, using DNS SRV records.

tldr.problem: The 'im' and 'pres' URI schemes name instant inboxes and presentities, but a client still needs a way to find the server that handles a given domain.
tldr.mechanism: The client looks up a DNS SRV record whose Service label is _im or _pres and whose Protocol label names the messaging protocol, for example _im._bip.example.com., falling back to an A record if no SRV record exists.
tldr.outcome: Clients can try several servers in order and pick a protocol they share with the target domain. IANA created two registries for the Protocol labels.

today: RFC 3861 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of how im and pres URIs are resolved through DNS SRV records.

sections.title: Why Addresses Need Resolving
sections.content:
The Common Profiles for Presence (CPP) and Instant Messaging (CPIM) define two URI schemes: im for INSTANT INBOXes and pres for PRESENTITIES, using the model of RFC 2778. This document gives rules for locating the resources behind these URIs via the Domain Name Service. The RFC says the rules could no doubt be applied to other URI schemes too.

The URIs are useful even without CPIM or CPP gateways, for example when one host supports several instant messaging applications, and they can also locate a gateway for a domain. In that case the DNS records serve a purpose similar to Mail Exchange (MX) records. The system relies on SRV records and address (A) records.
sections.plainLanguage: An instant messaging address says who you want to reach, but not where they are. This document explains how to find out where.

sections.title: Building the SRV Lookup
sections.content:
A client resolves the destination domain in the identifier to a relay system or a final target system. Only resolvable, fully-qualified domain names are permitted in an IM URI.

The Service field of the SRV record is _im for instant messaging and _pres for presence, matching the URI schemes. The Protocol field holds an IANA-registered label for the underlying messaging or presence protocol. For the inbox im:fred@example.com with a hypothetical protocol called BIP, the lookup is for _im._bip.example.com.. The same procedure applies to pres URIs with the _pres label.

A client that supports several protocols may make several SRV queries, in an application-specific order, until it finds one it shares with the target domain.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the kind of chat (im or pres), the chat language, and the domain together as one phone book entry, and look that entry up.

sections.title: Domain Name Lookup
sections.content:
Once the client identifies the domain, a DNS lookup MUST be performed. The names MUST be fully-qualified; inferring them from partial names or local aliases is a local matter.

The lookup first tries to find SRV records. If a CNAME record is found instead, the resulting domain is processed as if it were the initial one. If SRV records exist, a sender MUST NOT use any A records for that domain unless they are located through the SRV records. If there are no SRV records but there is an A record, it is treated as an implicit SRV record with a preference of 0 pointing to that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Look for the special phone book entry first. Only if there is none do you fall back to the plain address of the domain.

sections.title: Using the Results
sections.content:
The returned records specify the next-hop server, which may be a protocol gateway or the endpoint itself. Receiving systems list the transfer protocols by which they can be reached, directly or through a translating gateway, using combinations of Service and Protocol labels. Which transfer protocol to use is a local configuration option of each sending system. A gateway needs a separate record for each transfer protocol and domain pair that it serves.

A successful lookup can give a list of alternative addresses because of multiple SRV records. For reliable operation the client MUST be able to try each in order until a delivery succeeds. The client MAY have a configurable limit on how many it tries, but SHOULD try at least two. Priority and weight handling follows RFC 2782.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone book lists several places, you try them one after another until someone answers, and you should try at least two before giving up.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registries
sections.content:
The URI usage and DNS procedures add no security considerations beyond those of the instant messaging and presence requirements (RFC 2779) and the SRV specification (RFC 2782). Later registrations of Protocol labels for _im or _pres MUST explain any security considerations of using that protocol with SRV.

The document reserves the _im and _pres Service labels. IANA created two registries, the Instant Messaging SRV Protocol Label registry and the Presence SRV Protocol Label registry. Each entry has a label name and a pointer to a specification of how the protocol uses SRV, under the "specification required" rule of RFC 2434. Labels MUST begin with an underscore.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is risky here, but anyone adding a new chat language to the phone book must explain its own safety issues.
